title: Medieval empires
subtitle: Rulers, battles and wonders, 400 to 1600
about: Rulers, battles, capitals, great buildings and famous troops of the medieval world, from Attila to Bayinnaung, across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. Every fact was checked against English Wikipedia; legends are flagged as legends, and the Mali capital is marked as disputed.

cards.prompt: Peasant girl who led a French army to relieve the siege of Orléans in 1429
cards.note: Sold to the English and tried for heresy at Rouen, she was burned in 1431, aged about nineteen; she was canonised in 1920.

cards.prompt: Founder of the Mongol Empire, acclaimed as its ruler at an assembly in 1206
cards.note: Born Temüjin, he was buried on or near the sacred peak Burkhan Khaldun, but the details of his burial were kept secret.

cards.prompt: King of the Franks crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III in 800
cards.note: The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid sent him an elephant named Abul-Abbas, which arrived at Aachen in 802.

cards.prompt: Sultan of Egypt and Syria who retook Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187
cards.note: He gave so much of his wealth away that at his death in 1193 nothing was left to pay for his funeral.

cards.prompt: English king called 'the Lionheart', a leader of the Third Crusade
cards.note: Captured on his way home from crusade, he was held for ransom by Emperor Henry VI; as king he spent perhaps six months in England.

cards.prompt: Scottish leader who, with Andrew Moray, won at Stirling Bridge in 1297
cards.note: Captured near Glasgow in 1305 and handed to Edward I, he was hanged, drawn and quartered in London for treason.

cards.prompt: Ruler of the Huns who invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452
cards.note: According to Priscus, he died in 453 during the feast for his marriage to Ildico, after a sudden, severe bleed, perhaps a nosebleed.

cards.prompt: Grandson of Genghis Khan who founded the Yuan dynasty of China
cards.note: His summer capital, Shangdu, is the Xanadu of Western legend; his main capital, Khanbaliq, stood where Beijing is today.

cards.prompt: Prince of Wallachia nicknamed 'the Impaler' for his brutal punishments
cards.note: Dracula means 'son of Dracul', the name his father took on joining the Order of the Dragon; it probably inspired Bram Stoker.

cards.prompt: Byzantine emperor who rebuilt Hagia Sophia and codified Roman law
cards.note: During the Nika riots of 532 he considered fleeing the capital by sea; his wife Theodora apparently persuaded him to stay.

cards.prompt: Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople at the age of 21
cards.note: With a chain barring the Golden Horn, he had his lighter warships dragged overland on a wooden track into the harbour.

cards.prompt: Mali emperor whose lavish gold gifts in Cairo, on his 1324 pilgrimage, reportedly lowered gold's value
cards.note: He brought the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili to Mali and helped make Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.

cards.prompt: Holy Roman Emperor who drowned crossing a river on the Third Crusade in 1190
cards.note: Legend says he is not dead but asleep with his knights in a cave in the Kyffhäuser mountains, waiting to return.

cards.prompt: Castilian knight who captured Valencia in 1094 and ruled it until his death
cards.note: Legend says his widow Jimena had his armoured corpse tied onto his horse Babieca to rally Valencia's defenders.

cards.prompt: Aztec emperor when Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519
cards.note: His name means roughly 'he frowns like a lord'; he died in 1520 while a captive of the Spaniards.

cards.prompt: Turco-Mongol conqueror who captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid at Ankara in 1402
cards.note: Tamerlane comes from Persian Timur-i Lang, 'Timur the Lame'; Soviet scientists who exhumed him in 1941 confirmed his crippled right leg.

cards.prompt: Gothic king whose army sacked Rome in 410
cards.note: Legend says he was buried with treasure beneath the Busento riverbed, and the captives who dug the grave were killed.

cards.prompt: Founder of the Mughal Empire in India
cards.note: A descendant of both Timur and Genghis Khan, he wrote a vivid memoir, the Baburnama, in Chagatai Turkic.

cards.prompt: Korean admiral famed for his turtle ships against the Japanese invasions
cards.note: Once arrested, taken to Seoul in chains and tortured by his own government, he died from a gunshot at Noryang in 1598.

cards.prompt: Ninth Sapa Inca, who turned the small Kingdom of Cusco into an empire
cards.note: Most archaeologists believe Machu Picchu was built as his royal estate; pachakutiy means 'the turn of the world' in Quechua.

cards.prompt: Justinian's general who conquered the Vandal kingdom of North Africa
cards.note: A later legend says Justinian blinded him and left him a beggar; in fact he was restored to favour before dying in 565.

cards.prompt: Victor of the Genpei War who founded Japan's first shogunate
cards.note: He ruled from Kamakura, far from the imperial court at Kyoto; after his death his widow Hōjō Masako acted as regent.

cards.prompt: Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy from Ravenna between 493 and 526
cards.note: Raised as a hostage in Constantinople, he killed his rival Odoacer with his own sword at a banquet celebrating their treaty.

cards.prompt: Founder of the Mali Empire after defeating the Sosso king at Kirina
cards.note: In the epic told by griots, he could not walk as a child until one day he miraculously rose and walked.

cards.prompt: Umayyad commander who led the Muslim invasion of Visigothic Iberia in 711
cards.note: The Rock of Gibraltar is named after him: Gibraltar comes from the Arabic Jabal Tariq, 'mountain of Tariq'.

cards.prompt: Norman adventurer whose capture of Bari in 1071 ended Byzantine rule in Italy
cards.note: His nickname Guiscard is variously rendered 'the Resourceful', 'the Cunning', 'the Fox' or 'the Weasel'.

cards.prompt: Crowned 'King' of Poland in 1384 to stress her sovereign status
cards.note: Her marriage to Lithuania's pagan ruler Jogaila, who converted to Catholicism, linked the two realms; she was canonised in 1997.

cards.prompt: Hussite general who stayed undefeated in battle, even after going blind
cards.note: According to the chronicler Piccolomini, his dying wish was for his skin to be made into drums so he could still lead his troops.

cards.prompt: Grand Duke of Lithuania who led its forces beside Jogaila at Grunwald in 1410
cards.note: Poles stopped the envoys carrying documents for his coronation as King of Lithuania; he died in 1430 at Trakai, uncrowned.

cards.prompt: Rajput king who beat Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain in 1191, then lost there in 1192
cards.note: The later epic Prithviraj Raso tells how he eloped with Samyogita, daughter of his rival King Jayachandra of Kannauj.

cards.prompt: Rebel leader who drove out the Ming and became emperor of Đại Việt in 1428
cards.note: Legend says a golden turtle took back his magic sword in a Hanoi lake, now Hoàn Kiếm, 'Lake of the Returned Sword'.

cards.prompt: Burmese king who built the largest empire in Southeast Asian history
cards.note: Thais, his former enemies, still remember him as the 'Conqueror of the Ten Directions'; his empire included Ayutthaya and Lan Xang.

cards.prompt: Khmer king who won a nine-year war of succession and reigned until 1050
cards.note: Known as the 'King of the Just Laws', he had some 4,000 officials swear allegiance; the oath survives in inscriptions of 1011.

cards.prompt: Legendary 10th-century queen said to have laid waste to the Kingdom of Aksum
cards.note: Her story survives mainly in oral tradition; she is said to have destroyed Aksum's churches and tried to wipe out its royal dynasty.

cards.prompt: Cuman khan who led his people into Hungary after defeats by the Mongols
cards.note: Accused of aiding the Mongols, he and his retinue were massacred at Pest in March 1241 by a mob led by some barons.

cards.prompt: Peasant rebel, possibly a swineherd, who became tsar of Bulgaria in 1278
cards.note: The Byzantines nicknamed him Lakhanas, 'cabbage'; he beat both Byzantines and Mongols before the Mongols killed him in exile in 1281.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Hastings
cards.note: Harold had beaten Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge weeks earlier; the Bayeux Tapestry's arrow-in-the-eye figure may not even be him.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Fall of Constantinople
cards.context: Ottoman siege of the Byzantine capital
cards.note: It is said the last emperor, Constantine XI, threw aside his purple regalia and died leading the final charge in the streets.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Agincourt
cards.context: Hundred Years' War, under Henry V
cards.note: Fought on Saint Crispin's Day; English and Welsh archers made up nearly 80 percent of Henry's army, and French knights struggled through mud.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Tours
cards.note: Chroniclers later nicknamed the Frankish victor Charles 'Martel', the Hammer; Arabic sources call it the Battle of the Highway of the Martyrs.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Crécy
cards.context: Hundred Years' War, under Edward III
cards.note: The blind King John of Bohemia had his horse tied to his attendants' and charged into the fight; all were killed.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Bannockburn
cards.context: Robert the Bruce against Edward II
cards.note: On the first day, the lightly armed Bruce met the charging knight Henry de Bohun in single combat and killed him.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Stirling Bridge
cards.note: The Lanercost Chronicle claims Wallace had a strip of the dead English official Hugh de Cressingham's skin made into a sword belt.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Hattin
cards.note: The crusaders' relic of the True Cross was captured; Saladin spared King Guy, assuring him that 'kings do not kill kings'.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Manzikert
cards.note: Sultan Alp Arslan set his boot on the captured Emperor Romanos IV's neck, then treated him kindly and freed him a week later.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Fall of Tenochtitlan
cards.context: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
cards.note: Cortés had sloops built to blockade the island city, where a smallpox epidemic had already killed many of its leaders.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Grunwald (Tannenberg)
cards.context: Poland and Lithuania against the Teutonic Order
cards.note: Before the battle the Grand Master sent two swords as an insult; the 'Grunwald Swords' became a national symbol of Poland.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Kosovo
cards.note: Both Prince Lazar and Sultan Murad I died; it is the only time an Ottoman sultan was killed in battle.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Ain Jalut
cards.note: A feigned retreat by the Mamluk general Baybars helped trap the Mongols; it was the first major halt to their advance.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
cards.note: Jordanes says the Visigothic king Theodoric I fell in the fighting, possibly thrown from his horse and trampled by his own men.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle on the Ice (Lake Peipus)
cards.note: The famous image of knights drowning through breaking ice comes from Eisenstein's 1938 film Alexander Nevsky, not the medieval sources.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Cajamarca
cards.context: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
cards.note: Fewer than 200 Spaniards under Pizarro seized Atahualpa in the town plaza, though nearly 80,000 Inca troops were camped nearby.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: First Battle of Panipat
cards.note: The noise of Babur's cannon panicked the Delhi sultan's war elephants; Sultan Ibrahim Lodi died on the field with thousands of his men.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
cards.note: A local shepherd, Martín Alhaja, guided the Christian army through the Despeñaperros Pass to surprise the Almohad camp.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Legnica
cards.note: Duke Henry II the Pious was beheaded while fleeing, and the Mongols paraded his head on a spear before the town.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Mohi
cards.note: King Béla IV escaped to the island fortress of Trogir on the Adriatic coast and stayed there until the Mongols withdrew.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Nagashino
cards.context: Oda Nobunaga against the Takeda clan
cards.note: A captured messenger, Torii Suneemon, was told to shout that no help was coming; he shouted that it was, and was crucified.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Myeongnyang
cards.note: Yi Sun-sin had only 13 ships; Korean sources say between 120 and 133 Japanese ships took part in the fighting.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Lechfeld
cards.note: The captured Hungarian leaders were hanged at Augsburg; the victory ended major Magyar raids into Western Europe.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Bouvines
cards.context: Philip II of France against Emperor Otto IV
cards.note: The defeat so weakened England's King John, Otto's ally, that his barons forced him to agree to Magna Carta the next year.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Talas
cards.note: An 11th-century writer claimed Chinese prisoners taken here taught papermaking at Samarkand; historians now doubt the story.

cards.label: Year of
cards.prompt: Battle of Bạch Đằng (against the Yuan fleet)
cards.note: Prince Trần Hưng Đạo planted iron-tipped stakes in the riverbed; the falling tide left the Yuan fleet stranded on them.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Byzantine Empire
cards.note: Constantine rebuilt the old Greek city of Byzantium as 'New Rome', and it later took his own name.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Mongol Empire
cards.note: An enslaved Parisian goldsmith, Guillaume Bouchier, built a silver tree there whose golden serpents poured out drinks on command.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Inca Empire
cards.note: The empire's Quechua name means 'land of four parts'; the corners of its four regions met at this city.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Aztec Empire
cards.note: Built on an island in Lake Texcoco, it now lies beneath the historic centre of Mexico City.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Khmer Empire
cards.note: Its name simply means 'capital city' in Khmer; after Ayutthaya sacked it in 1431, its people moved south.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Carolingian Empire
cards.note: Its French name, Aix-la-Chapelle, honours the palatine chapel Charlemagne built there; Romans had earlier built spas at its warm springs.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Abbasid Caliphate
cards.note: Caliph al-Mansur founded the city in 762; for part of the 9th century the caliphs ruled from Samarra instead.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Umayyad Caliphate of al-Andalus
cards.note: Under Caliph al-Hakam II its royal library reportedly held 400,000 to 500,000 volumes, when Saint Gall Abbey owned just over 100.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Visigothic Kingdom of Hispania
cards.note: Earlier, before losing most of Gaul to the Franks, the Visigoths had ruled from Toulouse.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy
cards.note: When Belisarius took the city in 540, the Ostrogoths moved their capital to Pavia and fought on under Totila.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Mali Empire
cards.note: Historians dispute the site: proposals include Niani in Guinea, a town on the Niger, a moving court, or no fixed capital.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Bayinnaung's Toungoo Empire
cards.note: Tabinshwehti moved his capital here for its trade; it had been the capital of the conquered Hanthawaddy kingdom.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Imperial Japan
cards.note: Founded by Emperor Kanmu as Heian-kyō, 'tranquil capital', it was laid out on a grid modelled on Tang China's Chang'an.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Joseon Korea
cards.note: The new dynasty moved its capital here in 1394; Hanseong means 'fortress city on the Han River'.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Ottoman Empire before 1453
cards.note: Sultan Murad moved the Ottoman capital here from Bursa; Mehmed the Conqueror was born in the city.

cards.label: Capital of
cards.prompt: Tang dynasty China
cards.note: Records around 750 called it a 'million-man city'; modern estimates put its walled population at 800,000 to 1,000,000.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Hagia Sophia
cards.context: Byzantine domed church, now a mosque
cards.note: Designed by the geometers Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles, it was completed in 537 as the world's largest interior space.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Notre-Dame cathedral, damaged by fire in 2019
cards.note: One of the first buildings to use flying buttresses; after costly repairs to its roof and spire, it reopened in December 2024.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Angkor Wat
cards.note: Built for Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple to Vishnu, it gradually became Buddhist; it is the world's largest religious complex.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: The Forbidden City
cards.note: Built from 1406 to 1420 under the Ming, it was home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors until 1924.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Machu Picchu
cards.note: Its original Inca name may have been Huayna Picchu; the American historian Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: The Alhambra
cards.note: Its Arabic name means 'the red one'; it is one of the best-preserved palaces surviving from the medieval Islamic world.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Dome of the Rock
cards.note: Built for the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in 691 to 692 over the Foundation Stone, it is Islam's oldest surviving building.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Westminster Abbey
cards.note: Edward the Confessor built its first large church in the 1040s; coronations of English monarchs have taken place there since 1066.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: The Mezquita, a mosque turned cathedral
cards.note: Its signature rows of two-tiered arches reused Roman and Visigothic columns; Castile converted it into a cathedral in 1236.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Krak des Chevaliers
cards.note: The Mamluks took it from the Knights Hospitaller in 1271 after a 36-day siege, supposedly using a forged surrender order.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Borobudur
cards.note: This 9th-century temple carries 2,672 relief panels; the British administrator Thomas Stamford Raffles brought it to world attention in 1814.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Tōdai-ji
cards.note: Its Great Buddha Hall houses the world's largest bronze statue of the Buddha Vairocana, known in Japanese as the Daibutsu.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Shwedagon Pagoda
cards.note: Legend says it enshrines eight hairs of the Buddha; a Portuguese adventurer seized its huge bell, which fell into the Bago River.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Qutb Minar
cards.note: Aibak began it after the defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan but finished only the first storey; later sultans completed it.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Great Mosque of Djenné
cards.note: The townspeople repair it at an annual festival; the first mosque here dates from about the 13th century, the present one from 1907.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Temple of the Great Jaguar (Temple I)
cards.note: Named for a carved lintel showing a king on a jaguar throne; it is the funerary temple of the ruler Jasaw Chan K'awiil I.

cards.label: Where is
cards.prompt: Bete Giyorgis, the Church of Saint George
cards.note: One of eleven churches cut from solid rock; the town, once called Roha, was renamed after the Zagwe king Lalibela.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Hereditary warrior class of Japan, serving as retainers to their lords
cards.note: Their name probably comes from saburau, 'one who serves'; swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship were their primary martial skills.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Crusading military order, early bankers of Christendom, suppressed by the pope in 1312
cards.note: Their emblem of two knights sharing one horse stressed their poverty; Philip IV of France had many arrested in 1307.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Archers with bows about six feet long, decisive at Crécy and Agincourt
cards.note: About 137 bows survive, most recovered from Henry VIII's warship Mary Rose, which sank at Portsmouth in 1545.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Ottoman sultan's elite household infantry, recruited through the devshirme
cards.note: Their name means 'new soldier'; they were forbidden to marry until retirement and, unlike other Muslims, to wear beards.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Steppe riders who shot from the saddle as they conquered from China to Hungary
cards.note: Each rider kept three or four horses, changing mounts to travel fast for days; their composite bows were horn, wood and sinew.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: German crusading order that conquered and Christianised Prussia
cards.note: Founded around 1190 at Acre to aid pilgrims and run hospitals, the order still exists today as a Catholic religious institution.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Norse warriors said to fight in a trance-like fury
cards.note: Their name most likely means 'bear-shirt'; Snorri Sturluson's reading, 'bare-shirt', meaning without armour, is now largely abandoned.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Iberian adventurers who overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires
cards.note: Hernán Cortés and Francisco Pizarro were second cousins, both from Extremadura, where many of the Spanish conquerors were born.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Slave-soldiers, bought young and trained, who seized power in Egypt in 1250
cards.note: Their name means 'one who is owned'; they ruled Egypt as a sultanate from 1250 until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Byzantine emperors' axe-bearing bodyguard of Norsemen, later joined by Anglo-Saxons
cards.note: Harald Hardrada served in it before becoming King of Norway; Anna Komnene called its men 'axe-bearing barbarians'.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Heavy lancers with horse and rider both encased in armour
cards.note: Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas revived them in a blunt-nosed wedge; the historian Leo the Deacon called them 'fully iron-clad'.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Mercenary pike infantry from the Alpine cantons, hired across Europe for deep-column attacks
cards.note: Their German name Reisläufer means 'one who goes to war'; the Pontifical Swiss Guard at the Vatican is their last remnant.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Aztec elite warriors, admitted after capturing four enemies in battle
cards.note: Their animal represented the god Tezcatlipoca; they fought with the macuahuitl, a wooden club edged with obsidian blades.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Bohemian rebels' carts, chained into mobile forts bristling with hand cannons
cards.note: Their gun called píšťala, 'pipe', possibly gave us 'pistol', and their houfnice gave English the word 'howitzer'.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Italian mercenary crossbowmen, each with a big pavise shield, who fought for France at Crécy
cards.note: Each worked with two assistants, one holding the pavise and one spanning a second bow, doubling the rate of fire.

cards.label: Name the troops
cards.prompt: Disciplined royal bodyguards of Cnut the Great, later Harold's elite at Hastings
cards.note: A 12th-century Danish historian says Cnut's household warriors lived under their own law, the Witherlogh or Lex Castrensis.
